claim: Only a fraction of cancer patients benefits from immune checkpoint inhibitors.
source: Only a fraction of cancer patients benefits from immune checkpoint inhibitors.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that reflects established clinical knowledge about checkpoint inhibitor response rates.

claim: The dense extracellular matrix (ECM) forms a barrier for T cells in tumors.
source: This may be partly due to the dense extracellular matrix (ECM) that forms a barrier for T cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and established understanding in the field, as elaborated in the introduction.

claim: In vivo stiffness measurements are strongly correlated with tumor growth in the studied models.
source: In vivo stiffness measurements were found to be strongly correlated with tumor growth and ECM crosslinking but negatively correlated with T cell migration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A showing correlations between tumor stiffness and volume.

claim: In vivo stiffness measurements are strongly correlated with ECM crosslinking.
source: In vivo stiffness measurements were found to be strongly correlated with tumor growth and ECM crosslinking but negatively correlated with T cell migration.
evidence: This is supported by data showing collagen crosslink density measurements and stiffness correlations.

claim: In vivo stiffness measurements are negatively correlated with T cell migration.
source: In vivo stiffness measurements were found to be strongly correlated with tumor growth and ECM crosslinking but negatively correlated with T cell migration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing inverse correlations between tumor stiffness and T cell motility parameters.

claim: Interfering with collagen stabilization reduces ECM content in tumors.
source: Interfering with collagen stabilization reduces ECM content and tumor stiffness leading to improved T cell migration and increased efficacy of anti-PD-1 blockade.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced collagen fiber characteristics upon BAPN treatment in Figure 3.

claim: Interfering with collagen stabilization reduces tumor stiffness.
source: Interfering with collagen stabilization reduces ECM content and tumor stiffness leading to improved T cell migration and increased efficacy of anti-PD-1 blockade.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing reduced stiffness measurements upon BAPN treatment.

claim: Interfering with collagen stabilization leads to improved T cell migration.
source: Interfering with collagen stabilization reduces ECM content and tumor stiffness leading to improved T cell migration and increased efficacy of anti-PD-1 blockade.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing increased T cell motility parameters upon BAPN treatment.

claim: Interfering with collagen stabilization increases efficacy of anti-PD-1 blockade.
source: Interfering with collagen stabilization reduces ECM content and tumor stiffness leading to improved T cell migration and increased efficacy of anti-PD-1 blockade.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7A showing reduced tumor growth with combination therapy.

claim: Monoclonal antibodies blocking CTLA-4 and PD-1 have been approved as treatments for a significant number of tumors.
source: Monoclonal antibodies blocking the immune checkpoints cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen 4 (CTLA-4) and programmed death one receptor (PD-1) have quickly gone from proof of concepts to FDA-approved first- and second-line treatments for a significant number of tumors even in late stages (Callahan et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Callahan et al., 2016.

claim: An elevated percentage of patients with solid tumors fail to respond to immune checkpoint inhibitor therapies.
source: However, an elevated percentage of patients with solid tumors fail to respond to these therapies.
evidence: This is a well-established clinical observation supported by general knowledge in the field.

claim: T cell function and distribution in tumors are affected by numerous immunosuppressive mechanisms.
source: The mechanisms underlying the poor response to immune checkpoint inhibitors are still uncertain; nevertheless, recent results suggest that T cell function and distribution in the tumor are affected by numerous immunosuppressive mechanisms (Anderson et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Anderson et al., 2017.

claim: In progressing tumors, T cells exhibit a particular phenotype unable to normally respond to tumor antigens.
source: It is well established that in progressing tumors T cells exhibit a particular phenotype unable to normally respond to tumor antigens.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: In a large proportion of tumors, T lymphocytes are excluded from tumor cell regions in a so-called 'excluded-immune profile'.
source: In addition, in a large proportion of tumors, T lymphocytes are excluded from the tumor cell regions in a so-called 'excluded-immune profile' (Hegde et al., 2016; Herbst et al., 2014; Joyce and Fearon, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hegde et al., 2016; Herbst et al., 2014; Joyce and Fearon, 2015.

claim: Tumors enriched in T cells are more susceptible to be controlled by PD-1 blockade.
source: As a support for this notion, various clinical studies have shown that tumors enriched in T cells are more susceptible to be controlled by PD-1 blockade.
evidence: This is supported by clinical studies mentioned in the text.

claim: Tumors with immune-excluded profiles are refractory to PD-1 blockade.
source: In contrast, tumors with so-called immune-excluded profiles, in which T cells are present within tumors but not in contact with malignant cells, are refractory to PD-1 blockade (Herbst et al., 2014; Mariathasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Herbst et al., 2014; Mariathasan et al., 2018.

claim: The fibrotic state of desmoplastic tumors can cause immunosuppression through multiple mechanisms.
source: Particularly, the fibrotic state of desmoplastic tumors can cause immunosuppression through multiple mechanisms (Turley et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Turley et al., 2015.

claim: Collagen fibrils architecture has a detrimental impact on the migratory behavior of T cells in fresh human tumor explants.
source: By using dynamic imaging microscopy, we highlighted the detrimental impact of collagen fibrils architecture on the migratory behavior of T cells in fresh human tumor explants.
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors using dynamic imaging.

claim: A guiding strategy combined with a physical hindrance process restrains T cells from contacting tumor cells, leading to the T cell excluded profile.
source: Both a guiding strategy combined with a physical hindrance process has been shown to restrain T cells from contacting tumor cells, thus leading to the T cell excluded profile (Salmon et al., 2012; Peranzoni et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Salmon et al., 2012; Peranzoni et al., 2013.

claim: A dense fibrotic stroma raises physical obstacles to immune cell infiltration similar to stromal resistance to chemotherapeutics, antibodies, nanoparticles, or virus tumor penetration.
source: Hence, a dense fibrotic stroma could raise physical obstacles to immune cell infiltration similar to the previously established stromal resistance to chemotherapeutics, antibodies, nanoparticles, or virus tumor penetration (Netti et al., 2000; Stylianopoulos et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Netti et al., 2000; Stylianopoulos et al., 2018.

claim: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF) can have both direct and indirect effects on T cell infiltration and function.
source: In addition, cellular components of tumor-associated fibrosis, particularly the cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF), can have both direct and indirect effects on T cell infiltration and function (Turley et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Turley et al., 2015.

claim: T cells engineered to express a chimeric antigen receptor together with heparanase show enhanced infiltration into xenografted tumors and anti-tumor efficacy.
source: T cells engineered to express a chimeric antigen receptor together with heparanase, an ECM-degrading enzyme, show enhanced infiltration into xenografted tumors as well as anti-tumor efficacy (Caruana et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Caruana et al., 2015.

claim: TGFβ signaling pathway plays a major role in promoting T cell exclusion from tumor cells.
source: Recently, a major role for the TGFβ signaling pathway in promoting T cell exclusion from tumor cells has been demonstrated.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent citations to studies on TGFβ neutralization.

claim: Neutralizing antibodies against TGFβ reduce collagen I production in breast and colorectal mouse tumor models.
source: In breast and colorectal mouse tumor models, neutralizing antibodies against TGFβ were shown to reduce collagen I production, overcoming the T cell excluded profile and increasing the efficacy of anti-PD-L1 antibodies (Mariathasan et al., 2018; Tauriello et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mariathasan et al., 2018; Tauriello et al., 2018.

claim: Neutralizing antibodies against TGFβ overcome the T cell excluded profile in breast and colorectal mouse tumor models.
source: In breast and colorectal mouse tumor models, neutralizing antibodies against TGFβ were shown to reduce collagen I production, overcoming the T cell excluded profile and increasing the efficacy of anti-PD-L1 antibodies (Mariathasan et al., 2018; Tauriello et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mariathasan et al., 2018; Tauriello et al., 2018.

claim: Neutralizing antibodies against TGFβ increase the efficacy of anti-PD-L1 antibodies in breast and colorectal mouse tumor models.
source: In breast and colorectal mouse tumor models, neutralizing antibodies against TGFβ were shown to reduce collagen I production, overcoming the T cell excluded profile and increasing the efficacy of anti-PD-L1 antibodies (Mariathasan et al., 2018; Tauriello et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mariathasan et al., 2018; Tauriello et al., 2018.

claim: An immune mesenchymal subtype has been identified in cholangiocarcinoma, which is associated with TGFβ signature and poor tumor-infiltrating cells.
source: In cholangiocarcinoma, an immune mesenchymal subtype has been identified, which is associated with TGFβ signature and poor tumor-infiltrating cells (Job et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Job et al., 2020.

claim: The CXCR4/CXCL12 axis in breast metastasis is associated with both desmoplasia and absence of cytotoxic T lymphocytes in tumors from mice.
source: Other axes including the CXCR4/CXCL12 in breast metastasis and the focal adhesion kinase in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) have also been associated with both desmoplasia and absence of cytotoxic T lymphocytes in tumors from mice (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2019.

claim: Focal adhesion kinase in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is associated with both desmoplasia and absence of cytotoxic T lymphocytes in tumors from mice.
source: Other axes including the CXCR4/CXCL12 in breast metastasis and the focal adhesion kinase in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) have also been associated with both desmoplasia and absence of cytotoxic T lymphocytes in tumors from mice (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2019.

claim: Inhibition of CXCR4/CXCL12 and focal adhesion kinase axes in preclinical mouse cancer models reduces fibrosis while significantly increasing T cell infiltration.
source: Consequently, the inhibition of these axes in preclinical mouse cancer models was shown to reduce fibrosis while significantly increasing T cell infiltration and improving response to checkpoint inhibitors (Mariathasan et al., 2018; Tauriello et al., 2018; Incio et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mariathasan et al., 2018; Tauriello et al., 2018; Incio et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2016.

claim: Inhibition of CXCR4/CXCL12 and focal adhesion kinase axes in preclinical mouse cancer models improves response to checkpoint inhibitors.
source: Consequently, the inhibition of these axes in preclinical mouse cancer models was shown to reduce fibrosis while significantly increasing T cell infiltration and improving response to checkpoint inhibitors (Mariathasan et al., 2018; Tauriello et al., 2018; Incio et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mariathasan et al., 2018; Tauriello et al., 2018; Incio et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2016.

claim: Clinical trials testing combinations of stromal targeting with checkpoint inhibitors are currently ongoing in advanced pancreatic cancer, mesothelioma, urothelial carcinoma, and other malignancies.
source: Clinical trials testing such combination are currently ongoing in advanced pancreatic cancer, mesothelioma, urothelial carcinoma, and other malignancies (NCT02546531, NCT02758587, NCT02734160, NCT04064190, and NCT02947165).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to specific clinical trial identifiers.

claim: Tumor stiffness is considerably higher compared to neighboring healthy tissues in breast, colorectal, liver, and pancreatic tumors.
source: An important feature of fibrotic tumors is their considerable higher stiffness compared to their neighboring healthy tissues, which are highly correlated with cancer progression and metastasis, particularly in breast, colorectal, liver, and pancreatic tumors (Venkatesh et al., 2008; Samani et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Venkatesh et al., 2008; Samani et al., 2007.

claim: Tumor stiffness is highly correlated with cancer progression and metastasis in breast, colorectal, liver, and pancreatic tumors.
source: An important feature of fibrotic tumors is their considerable higher stiffness compared to their neighboring healthy tissues, which are highly correlated with cancer progression and metastasis, particularly in breast, colorectal, liver, and pancreatic tumors (Venkatesh et al., 2008; Samani et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Venkatesh et al., 2008; Samani et al., 2007.

claim: Shear wave elastography (SWE) allows accurate and non-invasive diagnostic and characterization of malignant lesions in vivo with prognostic significance in breast cancer.
source: The use of non-invasive imaging techniques such as shear wave elastography (SWE) and magnetic resonance elastography, designed to monitor stiffness of any given tissue, allows an accurate and non-invasive diagnostic and characterization of malignant lesions in vivo with prognostic significance, for instance in breast cancer (Evans et al., 2012; Song et al., 2018; Riegler et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Evans et al., 2012; Song et al., 2018; Riegler et al., 2018.

claim: Extensive remodeling of stromal components increases tumor stiffness and can mechanically activate intracellular signaling pathways that promote tumor progression.
source: Indeed, the extensive remodeling of the stromal components which increase tumor stiffness can mechanically activate intracellular signaling pathways that promote tumor progression and at the same time can dampen T cell functions including migration and infiltration into tumor islets (Datar and Schalper, 2016; Humphrey et al., 2014; Krebs et al., 2017; Rice et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Datar and Schalper, 2016; Humphrey et al., 2014; Krebs et al., 2017; Rice et al., 2017.

claim: Extensive remodeling of stromal components can dampen T cell functions including migration and infiltration into tumor islets.
source: Indeed, the extensive remodeling of the stromal components which increase tumor stiffness can mechanically activate intracellular signaling pathways that promote tumor progression and at the same time can dampen T cell functions including migration and infiltration into tumor islets (Datar and Schalper, 2016; Humphrey et al., 2014; Krebs et al., 2017; Rice et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Datar and Schalper, 2016; Humphrey et al., 2014; Krebs et al., 2017; Rice et al., 2017.

claim: LOX is a copper-dependent enzyme responsible for the crosslinking of collagen molecules into fibers.
source: In concert with these imaging biomarkers of both mechanical properties, ECM architecture, and T cell migration, we explored the consequences of altering the ECM by inhibition of the lysyl oxidase (LOX), a copper-dependent enzyme responsible for the crosslinking of collagen molecules into fibers that has been seen to be overexpressed in many metastatic tumors and responsible for malignant progression (Cox et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cox et al., 2016 and represents established biochemical knowledge.

claim: LOX is overexpressed in many metastatic tumors and responsible for malignant progression.
source: In concert with these imaging biomarkers of both mechanical properties, ECM architecture, and T cell migration, we explored the consequences of altering the ECM by inhibition of the lysyl oxidase (LOX), a copper-dependent enzyme responsible for the crosslinking of collagen molecules into fibers that has been seen to be overexpressed in many metastatic tumors and responsible for malignant progression (Cox et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cox et al., 2016.

claim: LOX inhibition has different mechanical modulating effects depending on the ECM architecture.
source: We highlight that LOX inhibition has different mechanical modulating effects depending on the ECM architecture, with significant improvement in T cell mobility.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing differential responses across tumor models in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: LOX inhibition results in significant improvement in T cell mobility.
source: We highlight that LOX inhibition has different mechanical modulating effects depending on the ECM architecture, with significant improvement in T cell mobility.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing increased T cell motility parameters.

claim: LOX inhibition alone has minor effects on primary tumor growth.
source: Despite minor effects in primary tumor growth upon LOX inhibition or PD-1 blockade treatment alone, their combination increases effector CD8 T cell accumulation in tumors and significantly delays tumor progression in a pancreatic cancer model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 supplements showing tumor growth curves.

claim: PD-1 blockade treatment alone has minor effects on primary tumor growth.
source: Despite minor effects in primary tumor growth upon LOX inhibition or PD-1 blockade treatment alone, their combination increases effector CD8 T cell accumulation in tumors and significantly delays tumor progression in a pancreatic cancer model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7A showing tumor growth curves.

claim: The combination of LOX inhibition and PD-1 blockade increases effector CD8 T cell accumulation in tumors.
source: Despite minor effects in primary tumor growth upon LOX inhibition or PD-1 blockade treatment alone, their combination increases effector CD8 T cell accumulation in tumors and significantly delays tumor progression in a pancreatic cancer model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7D showing increased CD8+ GrzmB+ T cells.

claim: The combination of LOX inhibition and PD-1 blockade significantly delays tumor progression in a pancreatic cancer model.
source: Despite minor effects in primary tumor growth upon LOX inhibition or PD-1 blockade treatment alone, their combination increases effector CD8 T cell accumulation in tumors and significantly delays tumor progression in a pancreatic cancer model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7A showing reduced tumor growth with combination therapy.

claim: In the EGI-1 cholangiocarcinoma model, tumor stiffening and tumor growth have a strong positive correlation.
source: In the EGI-1 cholangiocarcinoma model, tumor stiffening and tumor growth have a strong positive correlation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A displaying correlation plots.

claim: The EGI-1 model presents 20% of stiff regions (>40 kPa) on average that goes up to 50–60% in tumors with higher volume.
source: The stiffness distribution is highly heterogeneous, presenting 20% of stiff regions (>40 kPa) on average that goes up to 50–60% in tumors with higher volume.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from SWE measurements presented in the results.

claim: The EGI-1 model accurately reproduces the architecture of human cholangiocarcinoma.
source: This is a typical trait of desmoplastic tumors and the model accurately reproduces the architecture of human cholangiocarcinoma.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on histological observations and comparison to human disease.

claim: The EGI-1 collagen network is characterized by long (85.9 ± 42.0 µm) and thick (7.4 ± 2.2 µm) collagen fibers that are densely packed (6% of the tumor).
source: Its collagen network is characterized by long (85.9 ± 42.0 µm) and thick (7.4 ± 2.2 µm) collagen fibers that are densely packed (6% of the tumor) (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SHG imaging and Sirius Red staining.

claim: The KPC model exhibits a high positive correlation between tumor stiffness and volume.
source: The mouse PDAC KPC model (Hingorani et al., 2005) exhibits similar features to that of EGI-1. A high positive correlation between tumor stiffness and volume, presenting over 20% of stiff regions at high tumor volumes, was observed (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A displaying correlation plots.

claim: KPC tumors present typical segregation of ECM and tumor nests, with a high proportion of stroma (~20%).
source: KPC tumors present typical segregation of ECM and tumor nests, with a high proportion of stroma (~20%).
evidence: This is supported by histological observations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The KPC collagen network is characterized by shorter (67.1 ± 35 µm) and thinner (4.4 ± 0.9 µm) collagen fibers than that of EGI-1.
source: Its collagen network is characterized by shorter (67.1 ± 35 µm) and thinner (4.4 ± 0.9 µm) collagen fibers than that of EGI-1 (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SHG imaging.

claim: The MMTV-PyMT model stiffens during tumor progression.
source: The spontaneous orthotopic murine breast cancer model MMTV-PyMT, although slower in its growth as compared to subcutaneous tumors, also stiffens during tumor progression (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A displaying stiffness measurements over time.

claim: The MMTV-PyMT model has a lower density of stiff regions (<16%) compared to other models.
source: However, there is a lower density of stiff regions (<16%).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from SWE measurements.

claim: The MMTV-PyMT model presents a tumor islets-stroma structure with a lower amount of stroma (~13%) compared to EGI-1 and KPC models.
source: This spontaneous tumor model also presents a tumor islets-stroma structure, but with a lower amount of stroma (~13%) as compared to EGI-1 and KPC models.
evidence: This is supported by histological quantification.

claim: MMTV-PyMT collagen fibers are characterized for being thin (3.6 ± 1.1 µm) and long (83 ± 41 µm), forming densely packed regions taking up to 4.8% of the tumor.
source: Collagen fibers are characterized for being thin (3.6 ± 1.1 µm) and long (83 ± 41 µm), forming densely packed regions taking up to 4.8% of the tumor.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SHG imaging and Sirius Red staining.

claim: The mPDAC model has stroma that takes up ~40% of the tumor.
source: The stroma takes up ~40% of the tumor (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 2) but without clear spatial segregation of stromal and tumor compartments.
evidence: This is supported by histological quantification shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The mPDAC collagen network is made up of thin (3.5 ± 0.8 µm) and dispersed collagen fibers.
source: The mPDAC collagen network is made up of thin (3.5 ± 0.8 µm) and dispersed collagen fibers, which accounts for the lower presence of densely packed collagen regions (2.7% of the tumor).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SHG imaging.

claim: The mean tumor stiffness in mPDAC is lower than that of the other models.
source: The mean tumor stiffness is lower than that of the other models, partly explained by the limits of the maximal tumor volume reached in this orthotopic model (for ethical reasons) and partly by the collagen architecture.
evidence: This is supported by SWE measurements and is explained by both experimental limitations and structural features.

claim: Tumor stiffness increases with tumor volume in the mPDAC model.
source: Tumor stiffness also increases with tumor volume (Figure 1B) in line with previous studies performed in this model (Gilles et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B and a citation to Gilles et al., 2016.

claim: The MET-1 tumor model is characterized by low tumor stiffness.
source: Unlike the above-mentioned models that exhibit a high correlation between stiffness and tumor growth, the mouse breast carcinoma MET-1 tumor model is characterized by low tumor stiffness (Figure 1A), a limited stroma (~6%), the lack of tumor-islet/stroma organization, and the presence of thin (3.2 ± 0.9 µm) and dispersed collagen fibers (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by SWE measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The MET-1 model has a limited stroma (~6%).
source: Unlike the above-mentioned models that exhibit a high correlation between stiffness and tumor growth, the mouse breast carcinoma MET-1 tumor model is characterized by low tumor stiffness (Figure 1A), a limited stroma (~6%), the lack of tumor-islet/stroma organization, and the presence of thin (3.2 ± 0.9 µm) and dispersed collagen fibers (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by histological quantification.

claim: The MET-1 model lacks tumor-islet/stroma organization.
source: Unlike the above-mentioned models that exhibit a high correlation between stiffness and tumor growth, the mouse breast carcinoma MET-1 tumor model is characterized by low tumor stiffness (Figure 1A), a limited stroma (~6%), the lack of tumor-islet/stroma organization, and the presence of thin (3.2 ± 0.9 µm) and dispersed collagen fibers (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by histological observations in Figure 1C.

claim: In human breast cancer, a significant correlation between tumor stiffness and tumor size was demonstrated.
source: In human breast cancer, a significant correlation between tumor stiffness and tumor size was demonstrated (Evans et al., 2012; Song et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Evans et al., 2012; Song et al., 2018.

claim: Tumor stiffness measured non-invasively correlates with collagen accumulation associated with a segregated architecture of thick and densely packed collagen fibers surrounding tumor nests.
source: In addition, we show a correlation between tumor stiffness measured non-invasively with collagen accumulation associated with a segregated architecture of thick and densely packed collagen fibers (Sirius red positive) surrounding tumor nests.
evidence: This is supported by correlative data from SWE measurements and histological analysis.

claim: Tumors with an entangled and thin mesh of collagen fibers present lower rigidity despite overall high collagen content.
source: In contrast, tumors with an entangled and thin mesh of collagen fibers present lower rigidity despite overall high collagen content.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of different tumor models showing different stiffness despite similar collagen content.

claim: The appearance of stiff regions > 40 kPa is a physical biomarker of intratumor heterogeneity and ECM segregation.
source: Particularly the appearance of stiff regions > 40 kPa is seen as a physical biomarker of intratumor heterogeneity and ECM segregation.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the correlation between stiff regions and ECM architecture observed across models.

claim: BAPN is an inhibitor for LOX enzymatic activity.
source: Thus, we sought to determine whether beta-aminopropionitrile (BAPN), an inhibitor for LOX enzymatic activity, could modulate tumors' mechanical properties in concert with the stroma architecture (Levental et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Levental et al., 2009 and represents established knowledge.

claim: LOX stabilizes collagen fibers by enzymatic reactions that culminate in the formation of trivalent mature crosslinks including pyridinoline (PYD) and deoxypyridinoline (DPD).
source: LOX stabilizes collagen fibers by enzymatic reactions that culminate in the formation of trivalent mature crosslinks including pyridinoline (PYD) and deoxypyridinoline (DPD) (Yamauchi et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yamauchi et al., 2018 and represents established biochemical knowledge.

claim: PYD and DPD have intrinsic fluorescence that can be measured by two-photon microscopy.
source: PYD and DPD have an intrinsic fluorescence (Richards-Kortum and Sevick-Muraca, 1996), which can be measured by two-photon microscopy (Ex 720 nm, Em 400 nm) on tissue sections (Marturano et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Richards-Kortum and Sevick-Muraca, 1996; Marturano et al., 2014.

claim: The average fluorescence signals of PYD and DPD, measured in SHG-positive regions, were significantly decreased in BAPN-treated KPC tumors compared to control conditions.
source: Our data indicate that the average fluorescence signals of PYD and DPD, measured in SHG-positive regions, were significantly decreased in BAPN as compared to control conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: BAPN specifically blocks LOX enzymatic activity.
source: These results suggest that BAPN specifically blocks LOX enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduction in collagen crosslinks (PYD and DPD) upon BAPN treatment.

claim: All tumor models except MET-1 undergo a reduction in mean stiffness when LOX is inhibited.
source: Results show that all models, except for MET-1, undergo a reduction in mean stiffness when LOX is inhibited.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2A,C showing stiffness measurements.

claim: EGI-1 and KPC models show the most striking differences in stiffness upon LOX inhibition.
source: EGI-1 and KPC models both show the most striking differences (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2A,C showing stiffness measurements.

claim: In EGI-1 and KPC models, changes in stiffness are mainly perceived at late stages of tumor development.
source: Changes are mainly perceived at late stages of tumor developments since, in these models, tumor stiffness is positively correlated with tumor growth.
evidence: This is supported by the temporal analysis of stiffness data in Figure 2.

claim: In the MMTV-PyMT model, significant differences in stiffness were noted throughout the development of the tumor upon LOX inhibition.
source: In the MMTV-PyMT model, however, significant differences were noted throughout the development of the tumor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2A showing stiffness measurements at multiple timepoints.

claim: A significant decrease in mean tumor stiffness is seen in BAPN-treated mPDAC tumors.
source: For the mPDAC model, tumor stiffness was only evaluated at the end of the BAPN treatment. A significant decrease in mean tumor stiffness is seen in BAPN-treated mPDAC tumors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2A,C showing stiffness measurements.

claim: BAPN treatment did not affect tumor growth in most models.
source: Notably, BAPN treatment did not affect tumor growth in most models (Figure 2—figure supplements 2A–6A), except for mPDAC (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth curves shown in Figure 2 supplements.

claim: BAPN treatment affected tumor growth in the mPDAC model.
source: Notably, BAPN treatment did not affect tumor growth in most models (Figure 2—figure supplements 2A–6A), except for mPDAC (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth curves shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A.

claim: In both KPC and EGI-1 tumors, a clear difference in mean tumor stiffness can be seen in tumors with a volume > 400 mm3 upon BAPN treatment.
source: In both KPC and EGI-1 tumors, a clear difference in mean tumor stiffness can be seen in tumors with a volume > 400 mm3 (Figure 2—figure supplements 2C–3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 supplements showing stiffness at different tumor volumes.

claim: The percentage of control tumor area with a mean stiffness > 40 kPa increased with time within the non-treated tumor.
source: The percentage of control tumor area with a mean stiffness > 40 kPa increased with time (and with tumor volume) within the non-treated tumor indicating that there is not only an increase of overall mean stiffness but also an increase of the heterogeneity of stiff regions.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from SWE measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The percentage of tumor area with stiffness > 40 kPa was significantly reduced in BAPN-treated tumors.
source: However, this percentage was significantly reduced in BAPN-treated tumors with marked differences observed in the KPC model and to a lesser extent in EGI-1 and MMTV-PyMT models.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from SWE measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: BAPN-treated mPDAC tumors did not display stiff regions.
source: In mPDAC, BAPN-treated tumors did not display stiff regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B–D.

claim: MET-1 is the only model that does not respond to LOX inhibition by stiffness reduction.
source: The only model that does not respond to LOX inhibition by stiffness reduction is MET-1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 6B–C), in line with our previous data showing an absence of tumor stiffening during tumor growth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 6B–C.

claim: A significant reduction of collagen fiber width distribution was observed in EGI-1, KPC, and mPDAC models upon LOX inhibition.
source: A significant reduction of collagen fiber width distribution was observed in EGI-1, KPC, and mPDAC models, whilst fibers in the MMTV-PyMT tumor model did not display a significant change in their width (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SHG imaging shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fibers in the MMTV-PyMT tumor model did not display a significant change in their width upon LOX inhibition.
source: A significant reduction of collagen fiber width distribution was observed in EGI-1, KPC, and mPDAC models, whilst fibers in the MMTV-PyMT tumor model did not display a significant change in their width (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SHG imaging shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the EGI-1 model, collagen fiber width was decreased by 9.4% on average (6.7 µm versus 7.4 µm) upon LOX inhibition.
source: The most substantial difference was seen in the EGI-1 model, where collagen fiber width was decreased by 9.4% on average (6.7 µm versus 7.4 µm).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SHG imaging.

claim: Changes in collagen fiber width in mPDAC were 4.4% upon LOX inhibition.
source: Changes in mPDAC and KPC were less pronounced, with a reduction of 4.4% and 5%, respectively (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SHG imaging.

claim: Changes in collagen fiber width in KPC were 5% upon LOX inhibition.
source: Changes in mPDAC and KPC were less pronounced, with a reduction of 4.4% and 5%, respectively (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SHG imaging.

claim: The inhibition of LOX did not affect collagen fiber length in any of the models.
source: The inhibition of LOX did not affect collagen fiber length in any of the models (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SHG imaging.

claim: Collagen fibers in normal tissues are typically curly and anisotropic.
source: In general, the collagen fibers in normal tissues are typically curly and anisotropic in contrast to the situation observed in progressing tumors in which many of the fibers progressively thicken and linearize.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about tissue architecture.

claim: In progressing tumors, collagen fibers progressively thicken and linearize.
source: In general, the collagen fibers in normal tissues are typically curly and anisotropic in contrast to the situation observed in progressing tumors in which many of the fibers progressively thicken and linearize.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about tumor ECM remodeling.

claim: Fibers in non-treated tumors remained mainly oriented in one dominant direction with a CV from 1.85 to 0.5.
source: Fibers in non-treated tumors remained mainly oriented in one dominant direction (Figure 3B, C, and F) with a CV from 1.85 to 0.5 consistent with previous findings (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3B and a citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: LOX inhibition tends to disrupt the alignment of collagen fibers, making them more dispersed and oriented in different directions with increased CV.
source: LOX inhibition tends to disrupt the alignment of collagen fibers, meaning that they were more dispersed and oriented in different directions with increased CV as compared to control conditions.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The most significant effects of LOX inhibition on fiber orientation were seen in KPC and mPDAC models.
source: The most significant effects were seen in KPC and mPDAC models.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The curvature ratio of control tumors for all models was close to one, meaning that the collagen fibers were fully linearized.
source: The curvature ratio of control tumors for all models was close to one meaning that the collagen fibers were fully linearized.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: LOX inhibition severely affected fiber curvature, resulting in less linear and wavier fibers in all models.
source: In contrast, LOX inhibition severely affected fiber curvature, as there was a reversion of the fibers linearization resulting in less linear and wavier fibers in all models (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3D,F.

claim: LOX inhibition significantly decreased the surface covered by thick and densely packed collagen fibers in EGI-1, KPC, and MMTV-PyMT models.
source: Finally, LOX inhibition also significantly decreased the surface covered by thick and densely packed collagen fibers in EGI-1, KPC, and MMTV-PyMT model (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), correlating with the significant decrease in average tumor stiffness and in the proportion of stiff areas measured in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from Sirius Red staining shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The decrease in thick and densely packed collagen fibers upon LOX inhibition correlates with the significant decrease in average tumor stiffness and in the proportion of stiff areas measured in vivo.
source: Finally, LOX inhibition also significantly decreased the surface covered by thick and densely packed collagen fibers in EGI-1, KPC, and MMTV-PyMT model (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), correlating with the significant decrease in average tumor stiffness and in the proportion of stiff areas measured in vivo.
evidence: This is a correlative observation based on comparing histological and SWE data.

claim: Tumors treated with BAPN were softer than control ones in the KPC model, with mean stiffness of 1.80 ± 0.51 kPa compared to 4.15 ± 1.92 kPa for the control, as measured by plate shear rheometry.
source: It can be noted that tumors treated with BAPN were softer than control ones, with mean stiffness of 1.80 ± 0.51 kPa compared to 4.15 ± 1.92 kPa for the control.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from plate shear rheometry shown in Figure 4A.

claim: AFM measurements indicated that treatment of mice with BAPN leads to a narrower Young's modulus distribution shifted to lower values of elastic modulus (mean Young's modulus of 0.82 ± 1.58 kPa versus 1.70 ± 1.66 kPa).
source: AFM measurements indicated that treatment of mice with BAPN leads to a narrower Young's modulus distributions shifted to lower values of elastic modulus in comparison to the control samples (mean Young's modulus of 0.82 ± 1.58 kPa versus 1.70 ± 1.66 kPa, respectively) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from AFM measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: LOX inhibition reduces the high heterogeneity in local tissue mechanical properties of KPC tumor.
source: This confirms that the high heterogeneity in local tissue mechanical properties of KPC tumor can be reduced upon treatment with a LOX inhibitor.
evidence: This is inferred from the narrower distribution of Young's modulus values in BAPN-treated samples.

claim: The density and orientation of the ECM can have an important impact on T cell behavior and their displacement in fresh human lung and ovarian tumor slices.
source: Previous studies performed in our group have proved that the density and orientation of the ECM can have an important impact on T cell behavior and their displacement in fresh human lung and ovarian tumor slices (Salmon et al., 2012; Bougherara et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Salmon et al., 2012; Bougherara et al., 2015.

claim: Motile T cells were mainly found in loose ECM stromal regions, whereas fibrotic areas were devoid of lymphocytes.
source: Motile T cells were mainly found in loose ECM stromal regions, whereas fibrotic areas were devoid of lymphocytes.
evidence: This is based on previous observations from the authors' group.

claim: In control untreated tumors, T cells migrated slowly with average velocities ranging from 2.3 µm/min in the EGI-1 model to 4.1 µm/min in the MMTV-PyMT model.
source: In control untreated tumors, T cells migrated slowly with average velocities which were relatively homogeneous in the different models except in the mPDAC model (Video 1). Average velocities ranged from 2.3 µm/min in the EGI-1 model to 4.1 µm/min in the MMTV-PyMT model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dynamic imaging shown in Figure 5.

claim: The mean velocity of CD8 T cells in human lung tumors approaches 3 µm/min.
source: For example, the mean velocity of CD8 T cells in human lung tumors approaches 3 µm/min (Peranzoni et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Peranzoni et al., 2018.

claim: T cell track straightness indices are close to 0.4 in control tumors, consistent with previous reports on T cell displacements in tumors.
source: Analysis of T cell track straightness gives indices close to 0.4 consistent with previous reports on T cell displacements in tumors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and comparison to literature.

claim: In the mPDAC model, T cells were almost static during the 20 min recording (average speed of 1 µm/min and straightness of 0.1).
source: The mPDAC model differs from the others since T cells were almost static during the 20 min recording (average speed of 1 µm/min and straightness of 0.1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dynamic imaging shown in Figure 5.

claim: In every tested model, LOX inhibition resulted in an overall increase in T cell migration as compared to control conditions.
source: In every tested model, LOX inhibition resulted in an overall increase in T cell migration as compared to control conditions (Figure 5, Supplementary file 4 and Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dynamic imaging shown in Figure 5.

claim: In EGI-1 BAPN-treated tumors, activated PBT cells displayed longer displacement lengths compared to untreated tumors.
source: In EGI-1 BAPN-treated tumors, activated PBT cells displayed longer displacement lengths compared to untreated tumors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dynamic imaging shown in Figure 5.

claim: In MMTV-PyMT tumors, activated PBT cells displayed longer displacement lengths upon BAPN treatment.
source: This was also true for MMTV-PyMT tumors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dynamic imaging shown in Figure 5.

claim: In EGI-1 tumors, the trajectory straightness of activated PBTs was significantly increased upon LOX inhibition.
source: In EGI-1 tumors, the trajectory straightness of activated PBTs was also significantly increased upon LOX inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dynamic imaging shown in Figure 5.

claim: In both KPC and mPDAC models, LOX inhibition leads to an increase in the displacement of endogenous T cells.
source: We found that in both models, LOX inhibition leads to an increase in the displacement of T cells with a fivefold increase in the mPDAC model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dynamic imaging shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the mPDAC model, LOX inhibition leads to a fivefold increase in T cell displacement.
source: We found that in both models, LOX inhibition leads to an increase in the displacement of T cells with a fivefold increase in the mPDAC model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dynamic imaging shown in Figure 5.

claim: Enhancements in T cell speed were observed only in the mPDAC model upon LOX inhibition.
source: In terms of cell speed, enhancements were observed only in the mPDAC model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dynamic imaging shown in Figure 5.

claim: The trajectory straightness was increased in mPDAC models upon LOX inhibition, but not in KPC tumors.
source: Likewise, the trajectory straightness was increased in mPDAC models, but not in KPC tumors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dynamic imaging shown in Figure 5.

claim: BAPN treatment resulted in a threefold to fourfold increase of CD8+ T cells in both the stroma and tumor islets in KPC tumors.
source: By comparison, BAPN treatment resulted in a threefold to fourfold increase of CD8+ T cells in both the stroma and tumor islets (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: T cell motility was inversely correlated to tumor stiffness.
source: Our data indicate that T cell motility was inversely correlated to tumor stiffness (Figure 6) in line with Figure 5.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 correlating stiffness with T cell motility parameters.

claim: In three out of the four models tested, the correlation between T cell motility and tumor stiffness is different when comparing control and BAPN-treated tumors.
source: However, in three out of the four models tested this correlation is different if one compares control and BAPN-treated tumors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 showing different slopes for control vs. BAPN-treated tumors.

claim: In BAPN-treated tumors, there is a clear inverse linear correlation between T cell migration speed and mean tumor stiffness as evidenced by a steep slope.
source: In BAPN-treated tumors, there is a clear inverse linear correlation between T cell migration speed and mean tumor stiffness as evidenced by a steep slope.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Above a stiffness threshold that depends on the model, T cells are mostly arrested.
source: These results suggest that above a stiffness threshold that depends on the model, T cells are mostly arrested.
evidence: This is inferred from the non-linear relationship between stiffness and T cell motility shown in Figure 6.

claim: As tumor stiffness decreased by inhibition of LOX, T cell migration was restored.
source: In contrast, as tumor stiffness decreased by inhibition of LOX, T cell migration was restored.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased T cell motility in softer BAPN-treated tumors.

claim: T cell motility is highly influenced by small variations in the stiffness of softer tumors.
source: Thus, T cell motility is highly influenced by small variations in the stiffness of softer tumors as is the case when LOX's activity is inhibited.
evidence: This is inferred from the steep slope of the correlation in BAPN-treated tumors shown in Figure 6.

claim: PD-1 blockade did not affect tumor stiffness.
source: Unlike BAPN, PD-1 blockade did not affect tumor stiffness (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B) nor collagen organization including fiber orientation and curvature (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: PD-1 blockade did not affect collagen organization including fiber orientation and curvature.
source: Unlike BAPN, PD-1 blockade did not affect tumor stiffness (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B) nor collagen organization including fiber orientation and curvature (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The combination therapy of BAPN with anti-PD-1 was similar to that of BAPN alone on tumor stiffness and collagen organization parameters.
source: Moreover, the combination therapy was similar to that of BAPN alone on all of these parameters.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with single agents alone (BAPN or anti-PD-1) shows only non-significant reduction in tumor growth.
source: As shown in Figure 7A, while treatment with single agents alone only shows non-significant reduction in tumor growth, the combination of BAPN with the checkpoint inhibitor significantly delays tumor progression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The combination of BAPN with anti-PD-1 significantly delays tumor progression.
source: As shown in Figure 7A, while treatment with single agents alone only shows non-significant reduction in tumor growth, the combination of BAPN with the checkpoint inhibitor significantly delays tumor progression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: BAPN treatment alone significantly decreases the number of polymorphonuclear neutrophils.
source: We found that BAPN treatment alone significantly decreases the number of polymorphonuclear neutrophils (Figure 7B), but increases the presence of MHCII+ tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) (Figure 7C), while the combination therapy expanded the percentage of GrzmB CD8+ T cells (Figure 7D) and the ratio of CD8+ to Treg cells (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: BAPN treatment alone increases the presence of MHCII+ tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs).
source: We found that BAPN treatment alone significantly decreases the number of polymorphonuclear neutrophils (Figure 7B), but increases the presence of MHCII+ tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) (Figure 7C), while the combination therapy expanded the percentage of GrzmB CD8+ T cells (Figure 7D) and the ratio of CD8+ to Treg cells (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The combination therapy of BAPN with anti-PD-1 expanded the percentage of GrzmB CD8+ T cells.
source: We found that BAPN treatment alone significantly decreases the number of polymorphonuclear neutrophils (Figure 7B), but increases the presence of MHCII+ tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) (Figure 7C), while the combination therapy expanded the percentage of GrzmB CD8+ T cells (Figure 7D) and the ratio of CD8+ to Treg cells (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The combination therapy of BAPN with anti-PD-1 expanded the ratio of CD8+ to Treg cells.
source: We found that BAPN treatment alone significantly decreases the number of polymorphonuclear neutrophils (Figure 7B), but increases the presence of MHCII+ tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) (Figure 7C), while the combination therapy expanded the percentage of GrzmB CD8+ T cells (Figure 7D) and the ratio of CD8+ to Treg cells (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The combination therapy of BAPN with anti-PD-1 led to an increase in TNFα and RANTES.
source: Results show that the combination therapy led to an increase in TNFα and RANTES, supporting further the increase of T cell activation and infiltration and activation in this condition (Figure 7F–G).
evidence: This is supported by multiplex cytokine analysis shown in Figure 7F–G.

claim: In both BAPN and BAPN combined with anti-PD-1 conditions, an increase of GrzmB+ levels was observed compared to the control condition.
source: In both BAPN and BAPN combined with anti-PD-1 conditions, we observed an increase of GrzmB+ levels compared to the control condition (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by multiplex cytokine analysis shown in Figure 7H.

claim: LOX inhibition leads to an increase in T cell displacement within the KPC tumor.
source: Consistent with the data in Figure 5, LOX inhibition leads to an increase in T cell displacement within the KPC tumor (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dynamic imaging shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: PD-1 blockade alone produced a similar increase in T cell motility as LOX inhibition.
source: We also found that PD-1 blockade alone produced a similar increase in T cell motility, whereas the combination therapy showed the same effects as treatments alone (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dynamic imaging shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The combination therapy of BAPN with anti-PD-1 showed the same effects on T cell motility as treatments alone.
source: We also found that PD-1 blockade alone produced a similar increase in T cell motility, whereas the combination therapy showed the same effects as treatments alone (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dynamic imaging shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Features of wound healing and fibrosis are usually detrimental to anti-PD-1 responses, with the exception of desmoplastic melanomas.
source: With the exception of desmoplastic melanomas (Eroglu et al., 2018), features of wound healing and fibrosis are usually detrimental to anti-PD-1 responses (Hugo et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Eroglu et al., 2018; Hugo et al., 2016.

claim: In preclinical mouse tumor models, TGFβ inhibition with immune checkpoint blockade induces complete and durable responses in otherwise unresponsive tumors.
source: In preclinical mouse tumor models, TGFβ inhibition with immune checkpoint blockade induces complete and durable responses in otherwise unresponsive tumors (Mariathasan et al., 2018; Tauriello et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mariathasan et al., 2018; Tauriello et al., 2018.

claim: LOX inhibition in the transplanted KPC model increases the efficacy of anti-PD-1 treatment.
source: Our study indicates that LOX represents another valuable target as its inhibition in the transplanted KPC model increases the efficacy of anti-PD-1 treatment, while monotherapy with either agent alone is ineffective.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7A showing tumor growth with different treatments.

claim: Monotherapy with either LOX inhibition or anti-PD-1 alone is ineffective in the KPC model.
source: Our study indicates that LOX represents another valuable target as its inhibition in the transplanted KPC model increases the efficacy of anti-PD-1 treatment, while monotherapy with either agent alone is ineffective.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7A showing tumor growth with different treatments.

claim: The combination treatment of LOX inhibition with anti-PD-1 was associated with a tumor microenvironment shifted toward antitumoral effector cells and components, whereas immunosuppressive cells were reduced.
source: Moreover, the combination treatment was associated with a tumor microenvironment shifted toward antitumoral effector cells and components, whereas immunosuppressive cells were reduced.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 7B-E showing changes in immune cell populations.

claim: T cells preferentially accumulate and migrate in stromal regions that exhibited a loose matrix architecture but not in dense regions in human lung and ovarian tumors.
source: In human lung and ovarian tumors we found that T cells preferentially accumulate and migrate in stromal regions that exhibited a loose matrix architecture but not in dense regions (Salmon et al., 2012; Bougherara et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Salmon et al., 2012; Bougherara et al., 2015.

claim: In aged skin, dermal fibroblasts harbor a phenotype similar to CAFs and produce ECM matrices that limit T cell displacements.
source: Likewise, in aged skin, dermal fibroblasts harbor a phenotype similar to CAFs and produce ECM matrices that limit T cell displacements (Kaur et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kaur et al., 2019.

claim: In triple-negative breast cancers and in pancreatic tumors, T cells were still found in dense networks of collagen fibers.
source: However, in triple-negative breast cancers and in pancreatic tumors, T cells were still found in dense networks of collagen fibers (Li et al., 2019; Carstens et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Li et al., 2019; Carstens et al., 2017.

claim: T lymphocytes have the ability to adapt their morphology to the structure of the tissue up to a certain limit in 3D collagen matrices in vitro.
source: These data fit well with results obtained in vitro in a range of 3D collagen matrices showing that T lymphocytes have the ability to adapt their morphology to the structure of the tissue up to a certain limit (Wolf et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wolf et al., 2013.

claim: In dense collagen matrices, T cell motility is halted.
source: In dense collagen matrices, T cell motility is halted.
evidence: This is based on in vitro studies cited in the discussion.

claim: Anti-PD-1 treatment is associated with the production of IFNγ and inflammatory chemokines (e.g. CXCL10).
source: It is well established that anti-PD-1 treatment is associated with the production of IFNγ and inflammatory chemokines (e.g. CXCL10) that are presumably responsible for enhancing T cell motility in tumors (Peng et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Peng et al., 2012 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Fibrotic tumors are enriched in cells and factors that are known to impede T cells from migrating (e.g. hypoxia and tumor-associated macrophages).
source: A number of studies have shown that fibrotic tumors are, at the same time, enriched in cells and factors that are known to impede T cells from migrating (e.g. hypoxia and tumor-associated macrophages) (Manaster et al., 2019; Maller et al., 2021; Deligne et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Manaster et al., 2019; Maller et al., 2021; Deligne et al., 2020.

claim: LOX inhibition resulted in reduced angiogenesis according to previous studies.
source: As for possible effects of LOX inhibition on tumor blood vessels, previous studies have reported reduced angiogenesis after LOX and LOX-like protein inhibition and an increased perfused vessel density in the case of overexpression of LOX (Baker et al., 2013; Zaffryar-Eilot et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Baker et al., 2013; Zaffryar-Eilot et al., 2013.

claim: An increase in collagen crosslinking and matrix stiffness resulted in an increase in angiogenic sprouting.
source: However, other recent studies argue the opposite as an increase in collagen crosslinking and matrix stiffness resulted in an increase in angiogenic sprouting.
evidence: This is mentioned as contrasting evidence from other studies.

claim: The inhibition of collagen crosslinking in tumors resulted in reduced vascular density and permeability.
source: Conversely, the inhibition of collagen crosslinking in tumors resulted in reduced vascular density and permeability (Bordeleau et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bordeleau et al., 2017.

claim: LOX inhibition in a preventive setting is assumed to be most effective during early tumor stages when LOX activity is highest.
source: In this study, LOX inhibition was performed in a preventive setting. We assume that it is during early tumor stages and the construction of fibrous stroma that LOX activity is the highest.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the authors' reasoning about when LOX would be most active.

claim: In established tumors with significant levels of crosslinked collagen, LOX inhibition would have a more marginal effect.
source: In established tumors, with stroma having a significant level of crosslinked collagen, LOX inhibition would have a more marginal effect.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the authors' reasoning.

claim: Blocking LOX in combination with gemcitabine reduced metastases and increased survival of mice when treatment was started in the early stages of the disease, but not at later stages.
source: For example, blocking LOX in combination with gemcitabine reduced metastases and increased survival of the mice when treatment was started in the early stages of the disease, but not at later stages (Miller et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Miller et al., 2015.
